prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and opening new tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks rest on a simple and beautiful physical idea: at the magic wavelength the light shifts of the two clock states cancel, so thousands of atoms can be held in a lattice without the trap perturbing the transition. The uncertainty is then set by the atom and not by the apparatus. That is atomic structure and light-shift physics turned into an instrument, and it has delivered precision at the 10^-18 level that several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) have reproduced and compared over fibre and free space. This is the robustness I look for: many groups, agreement between theory and measurement, and a stable interpretation. The consequences are fundamental and not merely technological. They include tests of gravitational redshift at the millimetre scale, limits on drifts of constants, searches for ultralight dark matter, and the coming redefinition of the second. Katori made the proposal and the first realisations, and Ye took the system to record stability and developed the many-body picture of the clock. Two names give a clean allocation. I note the credited list is unusually unambiguous compared with the other candidates.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision-metrology recognition has already been given: the frequency comb in 2005 (Hall, Hansch) and ion-trap control in 2012 (Wineland, Haroche), and part of the committee may read the lattice clock as an incremental extension of honoured work rather than a new discovery. A second reservation is that priority and credit are shared with others, for example the SYRTE and PTB groups, the NIST ion-clock and Yb lattice work, and the theorists of magic wavelengths, and I am working from my own recollection of that history, not from documents. Finally, a prize could be seen as better timed after the redefinition of the second.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the IceCube astrophysical-neutrino result first as the opening of a new window on the universe, and ranks the Higgs discovery second as a measurement of first-rank importance, while placing the lattice clock fifth as clear and lasting but secondary.
responses.response: I agree that IceCube opens a genuinely new window and that the diffuse flux is a real discovery. My hesitation is the one Danielsson himself raises: only a few sources are firmly identified and the confirmation of the source associations rests largely on one detector, so the astrophysical meaning is still open, and the Halzen-Spiering split leaves out DUMAND and Baikal pioneers. For the clock, the independent reproduction is already complete and the physical interpretation is not in doubt. I would not say the clocks are the more important discovery, but I do think they are the more finished one. On the Higgs, I defer to him on particle physics, but he and I both see that three names cannot honestly represent two experiments of thousands, and that Virdee, Jenni and Della Negra are all arguably as strong. That structural obstacle seems to me a larger problem than any scientific doubt.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as the clearest new measurement technique and wonders whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second, while noting that the credit beyond Katori and Ye is blurred by other international clock groups.
responses.response: I share Kroll's ranking and his sense of what makes this attractive, but I would answer the waiting question differently. The redefinition is a metrological and administrative decision that depends on comparisons and roadmaps, and the science that deserves recognition, the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 systematic control, is already established. Waiting for a decision by the CGPM would tie a physics judgement to a standards process. I would also qualify his point on the other groups. Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow are important, but a prize must name at most three people and the line of invention (Katori's proposal, Ye's push to the limit) is the natural one. I do hold open that we may want to say in the citation that the achievement is the lattice-clock architecture and its precision, so that it does not appear to pass judgement on every group.

responses.point: Olsson ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy first as the decisive instrument advance for materials physics, with the lattice clock second, and she herself flags that an instrument invention may be weighed differently from a fundamental discovery and that Knut Urban may be missing from the trio.
responses.response: I respect the case for aberration correction: it is reproducible, ubiquitous and clearly overdue. Her own caveats are where I would press. The attribution problem is real: without Urban the TEM-corrector story is hard to tell, and the three credited names cannot be fixed from the provided record. I would also say that, as a theorist who is not a microscopist, I find the fundamental-physics content of a better lens harder to state than the content of the lattice clock, where the instrument itself is a test of quantum mechanics and relativity. I see the two as close in maturity, and I think she and I agree that the clock gives the cleaner statement. If the committee prefers a prize to materials physics, I would not oppose it but I would want Urban's role resolved first.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the topological insulator and quantum spin Hall prize first for its conceptual novelty and calls magic-angle graphene highly Nobel-worthy, while noting the incomplete credit (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, 3D work) and the unresolved superconducting mechanism in twisted graphene.
responses.response: I take his point that topological classification is a conceptual advance and not only a measurement, and I defer to him on condensed matter. But the same reservations he lists weigh on me: the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio omits the BHZ prediction that Molenkamp actually tested, and the 2016 prize already covered much of the topological ground. For twisted bilayer graphene I agree with his two-person theory-plus-experiment form, but the mechanism of superconductivity and the twist-angle disorder reproducibility concern are exactly the sort of open questions that make me prefer waiting. I would keep B022 as an alternative because the physics is remarkable, not because I think it is ready.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a basic-physics demonstration that became the common architecture of superconducting devices, and ranks the lattice clock seventh on the grounds that it may be an incremental extension of the comb and ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: The overlap worry is serious and I have listed it as my main reservation, but I do not think it is decisive. The comb gave a way to count optical cycles, and the ion work gave quantum control of single particles; neither gave a many-atom clock whose accuracy is not limited by the trap, which is the new physical idea. On circuit QED, I agree with him that the physics (strong light-matter coupling and dispersive readout) is distinct from the 2025 prize, but a trio that omits Wallraff, which he himself concedes, and the closeness to last year's prize make me cautious. He also tells us he has professional closeness to the field, which is the kind of disclosure I find useful.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee gives to the prior recognition of frequency combs (2005) and ion-trap quantum control (2012) when judging whether optical lattice clocks are a separate achievement.

Whether the history of priority between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and parallel work (SYRTE, PTB, NIST, other Sr and Yb groups) supports exactly these two names; I am working from recollection.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should affect the timing.
Whether the two-name configuration should be kept, or whether a combination with a second distinct achievement such as cold-atom lattice simulation would be more balanced.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. I should note that I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier and have worked with Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of these links involve the lattice-clock candidates. I have no personal tie to the B046 or B022 candidates either, though as an atomic theorist I work near the cold-atom field, so I should say that.
